groups.title: Products and apps
projects: Two-minute skill checks in 40-plus fields, scored Elo-style, with peer percentiles and three LLM features. Full stack on $0 a month.
EV trip planner for a five-year-old battery: range adjusted for elevation and weather, and a detour budget for avoiding risky turns.
What it takes to be top 1%, top 10% or median: 950 graded facts, and a question box with an opt-in MiniLM parser that runs in your browser.
Any picture or prompt becomes one continuous line, drawn by a chain of rotating arrows in the browser.
Today's Hong Kong news rewritten into spoken Cantonese, with neural audio, jyutping and speech grading. Rebuilt daily.
A tutor built from any Chinese EPUB: pinyin over every character, read-aloud, and offline pronunciation grading.

groups.title: The fine-tuning series
projects: Wine label photo to a cited profile and pairings; a 1.5B LoRA names the grape from a blind tasting note.
Menu photo to translated dishes with 14-allergen tags. A LoRA behind two guard layers that only add warnings: hidden misses on 60 adversarial dishes went from 22 to 0.
Receipt photos to categorized spending; 90.5% category accuracy on merchants the model never saw.
Course map photo to a km-by-km pacing plan that has to pass six deterministic checks.

groups.title: Retrieval and agents
projects: Hybrid search over 30,000 wine reviews that reads price, place and grape from the request first: limit-breaking results 77.5% to 0. Also runs in your browser.
A coach that calls my pace and heat models as tools, also served over MCP. On 42 frozen numeric checks it got 42 right, against 21 for plain RAG and 14 for the bare model.
A LangGraph agent whose self-critique is a schema-checked rubric: 10 of 10 dishes pass, every run replayable node by node.
A LangGraph agent that drafts a training plan and keeps revising it until it passes explicit safety checks.

groups.title: Running and athletics
projects: 80 Boston Marathons against ERA5 course weather: heat is free to 55°F, then costs about 0.4% of finish time per degree, with a live race-day forecast.
Only 2.5% of 31,912 Boston 2014 finishers ran a negative split; across eight Boston years the share runs from 2.4% to 10.8%.
Eight Boston years of 5 km splits and a live race predictor: enter splits as you pass each mat for a finish range and wall risk, tested on 2024.
Where any marathon time sits among 31,842 finishers, and how far out the world record is, using extreme-value theory.
Are Boston qualifying times equally hard for every age and gender group?
Three ways to rank the six Majors by difficulty, tested on simulated races with planted penalties.
How much of the recent drop in marathon times comes from the shoes.
Every Olympic event's world-record progression, a frailty survival model tested on 2011 to 2025, and the odds each current record falls before LA 2028.
Kruskal-Wallis tests on 6,400 elite marks: the best in some events score 68 points more than in others.
K-means and PCA on 43 nations across five disciplines, which fall into five profiles.

groups.title: Wine, words and money
projects: Nothing in about 120,000 unique reviews scores below 80, and 85% land between 84 and 92.
A season 1 °C warmer than normal moved scores by 0.24 points in cool regions, across 55,597 reviews and 55 regions. The checks weaken even that.
Hong Kong's five petrol brands post one price on 88% of days. Six years of posted prices screened against import costs, with Perth and Los Angeles for contrast.
Half the extra Wikipedia attention a death brings is gone about two days after the peak; a year later the page still draws 1.08 times its old traffic. 1,905 deaths and 178 awards, 2016 to 2025.
Fifty years of Billboard hits got longer and more repetitive, but the vocabulary held.
The top 100 words make up 61% of everything said; about 1,250 words cover 95%.
Grade level, vocabulary richness and a word-coverage curve for any EPUB, computed in the browser.
Replays a retirement plan through every start year since 1871. Ask it in plain English: an agent fills the scenario and the engine does all the math (also an MCP server).

groups.title: Small tools
projects: When to leave to arrive on time, from Google Maps traffic estimates.
A 45-minute layover at a US hub missed 17% of the time, from 23 million flights. Paste an itinerary and an agent scores each connection with the model.
A desktop app for read-along audiobooks in English, Mandarin and Cantonese.
A whole book becomes a two-host episode where every claim cites its source. Its checkers were tested on 56 lines broken on purpose: Opus caught all 56.
Terminal trivia while a slow build runs, now also a Claude Code plugin whose hooks open a companion pane while a tool call or subagent works.

selected.label: Full-stack product
selected.headline: Skill checks scored like chess ratings
selected.text: SkillCompass gives two-minute quizzes in more than 40 fields and scores each answer Elo-style against the item's difficulty. You get a percentile against other test-takers, a map of what you know and a study plan. The backend is FastAPI on free tiers, so it costs nothing to keep running.
selected.figcap: SkillCompass, captured from the live site.

selected.label: Agents and MCP
selected.headline: A coach that calls the models before it answers
selected.text: The same Claude model answers marathon questions three ways: on its own, with retrieval, and with my pace and heat models as tools (also served over MCP). On 42 numeric targets from a question set frozen before any run, the tool coach got 42, retrieval 21 and the bare model 14. A question costs a median 1.7 cents at API prices and takes 8.4 seconds; the write-up shows a full tool-call trace and where each system fails.
selected.figcap: Numeric answers within tolerance, by question type.

selected.label: Grounded generation
selected.headline: A two-host episode where every claim cites its source
selected.text: Podcastify turns a whole book or article into a two-host episode. Each factual line carries the ids of the sentences it rests on and is checked before it is voiced. Across four sources it covered 7.4 of 12 frozen key points against 4.4 for a rule-based script. An independent Opus check found 8 of 172 lines not fully supported, and the repair step did not lower that, which the page says plainly.
selected.figcap: Key-point coverage and unsupported lines, by source.

selected.label: Decision tool
selected.headline: Route planning for a five-year-old battery
selected.text: Leeway plans from the range your car has now, after five years of battery wear, and adjusts it for hills and weather. It keeps a hard reserve at every charger stop and spends a detour budget you set on avoiding unprotected left turns and rail crossings.
selected.figcap: Leeway's trip view, from its write-up.

selected.label: Survival analysis
selected.headline: Which world records fall before LA 2028?
selected.text: I rebuilt the ratified progression of all 46 Olympic events from World Athletics' records handbook, 1,251 reigns in all, and fitted a survival model with a frailty for each event. Fitted on what was known in 2010, it ranked the records that fell from 2011 to 2025 better than the base rate (Brier 0.235 against 0.329). Duplantis's pole vault leads the LA 2028 watchlist at 48%.
selected.figcap: The top of the LA 2028 watchlist, from the write-up.

series.intro: Four photo-to-data apps. Each pairs an LLM pipeline with a small Qwen2.5 model I fine-tuned on my laptop (LoRA) for one step of the task, then benchmarks base, fine-tuned and Claude zero-shot on held-out data.

notes.a: Clean rerun on 2026-10-28: Claude saw only the merchant text and the 12 labels, with tools off. Most of its misses are noisy labels in the test set (hardware and cables marked other). The first run scored 56.0% with a leaked category list.
notes.b: Scored on the same 200 notes, the fine-tuned model is right on 55 and Claude on 46 (sign test p = 0.33), so the gap is within noise.
notes.c: Claude needs the full allergen schema in every prompt to get there; the fine-tuned model gets the dish name only.

stories.headline: The 100-point wine scale is an 8-point scale
stories.text: Across about 120,000 unique professional reviews (the source file repeats 9,983) nothing scores below 80, and 85% land between 84 and 92. Some critics are simply more generous than others.

stories.headline: Predicting the wall from the first few splits
stories.text: A model trained on 176,059 Boston finishers from 2014 to 2023 reads your splits as you pass each mat and gives a finish range and the chance of hitting the wall. On the unseen 2024 race it missed by 7.9 minutes at halfway, against 18.1 for even pace.

cases.label: Guardrails
cases.headline: An allergen tagger that is only allowed to add warnings
cases.figcap: Dish inspector from the write-up: each allergen, its label, and what each guard layer raised.
cases.problem: A 1.5B model I fine-tuned to tag 14 allergens called a dish safe when it was not 7.3% of the time, and never flagged sulphites.
cases.built: Two layers behind it that can raise a warning but never lower one: a 541-word ingredient lexicon, then a Claude Haiku second opinion on whatever is still unflagged, schema-validated with a retry.
cases.result: Held-out false-safe 7.3% to 0.8%; hidden allergens missed on 60 adversarial dishes, frozen before the run, 22 to 0. The Haiku layer costs $0.18 per 1,000 dishes.
cases.failure: Over-warning rises to 27% on the adversarial set, and one of three Haiku runs cleared hummus of sesame.
cases.next: Human labels on the 840-row sheet in the repo, then distill Haiku's flags back into the small model.

cases.label: Judge evaluation
cases.headline: Testing the fact-checkers on lines broken on purpose
cases.figcap: Span viewer from the write-up: a script line, the source sentences it cites, and each judge's verdict.
cases.problem: Every line of a generated podcast cites its source sentences and is checked before it is voiced, but my old sample had one failure in 20, so it could not measure misses.
cases.built: A frozen set of 124 lines, 56 of them broken by code (a flipped negation, a moved number, a swapped name), so the right answer is known without labeling. Eight judge runs across Haiku, Sonnet and Opus, plus the local checks.
cases.result: Opus caught 56 of 56 broken lines in both runs; my pipeline's Sonnet checker caught 44 to 49, missing only negations. A majority vote did worse than Opus alone.
cases.failure: A JSON parser bug had left 33 lines unchecked on one run; fixed. An earlier page called a model's reading a hand check; corrected with a dated note.
cases.next: Subtler model-written breaks, human labels, and a Haiku-then-Opus cascade.

cases.label: Agent and MCP
cases.headline: A retirement agent that is not allowed to do arithmetic
cases.figcap: Recorded run from the write-up: question, extracted scenario, engine call, checked answer.
cases.problem: People ask retirement questions in sentences, and a bare model answers them with numbers it made up.
cases.built: Claude fills a validated JSON scenario, code runs my 152-year simulation engine, and the reply is rejected if it holds any number the engine did not produce. The engine is also an MCP server.
cases.result: 28 of 30 frozen questions right end to end; the headline answer matched the engine on 19 of 20, against 3 of 20 for the bare model, with 1 unsourced number in 300 against 127 in 289. $0.009 and 7.7 s a question.
cases.failure: One reply dropped the what-if result entirely; my check passes it, because nothing was invented.
cases.next: A check that every headline value appears in the reply, and human labels for the expected scenarios.

cases.label: RAG and in-browser search
cases.headline: Reading 'under twenty bucks' out of the sentence before ranking
cases.figcap: In-browser search from the write-up: MiniLM runs in the page, filters read from the request.
cases.problem: My hybrid retriever ignored plain-English limits: on 28 frozen requests, 77.5% of top-ten results broke a stated price, place or grape.
cases.built: A pydantic schema Claude fills, checked against the index's own vocabulary with one repair, applied as filters before dense, BM25 and reranking. The same search also runs in your browser on a self-hosted MiniLM.
cases.result: Limit-breaking results 77.5% to 0 with Sonnet ($0.05 a request) and 1.2% with Haiku ($0.003). The browser index matches the Python retriever on 8.8 of the top 10.
cases.failure: A regex extractor tied Sonnet, but I wrote both the rules and the requests; the 'not oaky' filter drops unoaked Chardonnays.
cases.next: Requests written by someone else, and wiring extraction into the command line.

cases.label: Agent self-critique
cases.headline: A self-critique that never passed, rebuilt as a rubric
cases.figcap: Trace replay from the write-up: each node's timing, the tool call and the critique JSON.
cases.problem: My LangGraph pairing agent rejected all 12 of its own drafts, mostly for wines it judged too old as of 2026.
cases.built: A seven-criterion rubric: three checked in code, four graded by the model as schema-validated JSON, with the pass decided in code. Every run is saved and replayable node by node.
cases.result: 10 of 10 frozen dishes pass, every first pick an accepted grape against 3 of 10 for plain search. Cost $1.25 to $0.49 and time 78 s to 34 s per pairing. It rejected 6 of 6 deliberately mismatched drafts.
cases.failure: A second judge on Sonnet agreed on only 6 of 10 verdicts (kappa 0.20), and caught a reply telling a guest about 'the Sancerre style you're after'.
cases.next: Human labels from the sheet in the repo, and a code check for claims against the cited review.

changelog.html: Ten projects upgraded: guard layers and an adversarial set for Menu Decoder, judges tested on deliberately broken lines for Podcastify, agents that call my own models for the retirement and connection tools (both also MCP servers), constraint extraction and in-browser search for Wine RAG, a rubric critic for the pairing agent, an in-browser parser for One in a Hundred, a Claude Code plugin for downtime, plus red-teaming and schema-checked plans for the two marathon agents. Every project has a demo video.
Tests on GitHub Actions for 13 repos; fresh-clone runs of 25 READMEs fixed; cost and latency measured for the agents and the fine-tuning series.
Result-first write-ups with error analysis; Wine RAG re-evaluated on 30 new frozen queries, and an earlier claim about BM25 fusion withdrawn.
Audit of three new studies: a duplicated source file and a wrong API date found and fixed, with dated notes on the pages.
Six studies rebuilt into tools: a pacing predictor tested on Boston 2024, an 80-race heat model, a record-survival model backtested on 2011 to 2025, and the tool-calling coach with its MCP server.
